schema: cards = [text, seconds, kind]; kind: hook | body | quote | cite | cta. hook_b = test variant for T1. source.type: quote (verbatim, public-domain translation) | idea (modern book, Moodius words, no quotation) | data | original

scripts.hook: You'd never let a stranger decide what you're worth.
scripts.hook_b: Marcus Aurelius noticed a strange habit. You have it.
cards: You'd never let a stranger decide what you're worth.
Then you post something and refresh it forty times.
Marcus Aurelius noticed it 1,800 years before likes:
“Every man loves himself more than all the rest of men, but yet sets less value on his own opinion of himself than on the opinion of others.”
Before you check what they think, ask what you think.
Send this to the friend who refreshes.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate. Hook top-left on the 96px margin, Ember rule under it. Quote card in Playfair italic.
scripts.caption:
Likes are a vote from people who gave your post half a second. Your own opinion of you has watched every day of your life.

Marcus wrote this with no phone, about the same habit. Tonight, before you open the app, answer one thing: what do you actually think of what you made?

— Moodius
scripts.first_comment: What would you post if nobody could see the likes?

scripts.hook: Kafka wrote the most accurate book about work.
scripts.hook_b: A man wakes up as a giant insect. Guess what he worries about.
cards: Kafka wrote the most accurate book about work.
A man wakes up as a giant insect.
And what does he worry about?
Idea: Franz Kafka, The Metamorphosis (1915) · Moodius reading
If your first thought while falling apart is your boss, look at that.
Send this to someone who answered emails with a fever.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate, or V2 footage tag 'commute' (train window, platform at dawn). Punchline cards 4-5 in display serif.

source.author: Franz Kafka
source.section: Part I (Gregor's first thoughts are his job and the train he has missed)

scripts.caption:
Gregor Samsa turns into an insect overnight, and his first real panic is that he's late and the office will notice.

It's a joke, and it isn't. If the job is the first thing you think of when you're ill, grieving or falling apart, it has more of you than it paid for.

What's one thing you'd stop doing if work didn't count tomorrow?

— Moodius
scripts.first_comment: Kafka worked in an insurance office for most of his life. He wrote at night.

scripts.hook: Solitude: your phone is off.
scripts.hook_b: There are two ways to be alone. Only one of them is good.
cards: Loneliness: your phone is on. And quiet.
One you choose. The other happens to you. From the outside they look the same.
1 in 4 young men in the US felt lonely for a lot of yesterday.
Text one person today. Not a meme. A sentence.
Save this for a quiet night.
scripts.visual: V2 footage tag 'phone-table' (phone face up on a table at night, screen dark), Slate overlay 72%. Fallback V1.

source.author: Gallup
source.work: Younger Men in the U.S. Among the Loneliest in West (May 2025)
source.section: 25% of US men aged 15-34 felt lonely 'a lot of the day yesterday'

scripts.caption:
Being alone isn't the problem. Being alone when you didn't choose it is.

If the quiet lately is the second kind, you're not broken and you're not rare. A quarter of young men in the US said they felt lonely for a lot of the previous day (Gallup, 2025).

The fix is smaller than it feels: one real sentence to one real person. Who's the first name that came to mind?

— Moodius
scripts.first_comment: Solitude you choose recharges you. Loneliness drains you. If you can't tell which one this is, ask: would I pick up if someone called?

scripts.hook: The first year of getting better looks embarrassing.
scripts.hook_b: If they're laughing at your new habits, read this.
cards: The first year of getting better looks embarrassing.
Water at the bar. Leaving early. Reading on the train like a weirdo.
“If you would improve, submit to being considered senseless and foolish with respect to externals.”
Being laughed at for a year is cheaper than staying the same for ten.
Save this for the next time they laugh.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate.
scripts.caption:
Nobody warns you that the early version of a better life looks a bit ridiculous from the outside. You'll be the one leaving at eleven, the one who doesn't drink, the one with the book.

Epictetus told his students to accept looking foolish about things that don't matter. The ones laughing are usually watching closely.

What's the habit you'd start if nobody could see?

— Moodius
scripts.first_comment: It gets quieter around month four. People stop commenting and start asking.

scripts.hook: You want to be chosen. You don't choose anyone.
scripts.hook_b: Seneca found the only love potion that works.
cards: You want to be chosen. You don't choose anyone.
You wait for them to text first, then call it being independent.
Seneca found the answer in an older writer, Hecato:
“I can show you a philtre, compounded without drugs, herbs, or any witch's incantation: ‘If you would be loved, love.’”
Go first. It isn't needy. It's how it starts.
Send this to someone. Go first.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate. Optional V2 tag 'two-cups' (two mugs on a table).
scripts.caption:
There's a version of independence that's really just fear with good posture. You don't reach out, so you can't be turned down.

Seneca's answer is two thousand years old and still annoyingly simple. If you want people close, be the one who moves closer.

Who have you been waiting on to message first?

— Moodius
scripts.first_comment: Going first doesn't mean going all in. It means one honest message.

scripts.hook: Angry men are usually something else first.
scripts.hook_b: You were probably taught one feeling. Here's what it hides.
cards: Angry men are usually something else first.
Many boys learn that anger is the one feeling they're allowed to show. So everything comes out as anger.
Idea: bell hooks, The Will to Change (2004) · Moodius words
Next time it rises, ask one question: what's under this?
Name that. Then decide what to do.
Save this. Use it once this week.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate. Card 2 words appear one by one (0.5s each) in Bone; 'Ignored.' in Ember.

source.author: bell hooks
source.work: The Will to Change: Men, Masculinity, and Love
source.section: argument that boys are allowed anger and taught to hide other feelings

scripts.caption:
If anger was the only feeling that was safe to show growing up, it ends up carrying everything else: the hurt, the shame, the fear.

That's not a character flaw. It's a habit you were handed. You can put some of it down by naming what's underneath before you act.

What's usually under yours?

— Moodius
scripts.first_comment: Marcus Aurelius wrote about anger more than almost anything else. He wasn't calm by nature either.

scripts.hook: Try sitting alone for five minutes. No phone.
scripts.hook_b: In a study, people chose electric shocks over this.
cards: Try sitting alone for five minutes. No phone.
Notice how fast your hand goes to your pocket.
Pascal saw it in the 1600s, without a pocket:
“…all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber.”
Pascal, Pensées 139 · tr. W. F. Trotter
The phone isn't the problem. The quiet is. Practise the quiet.
scripts.visual: V2 footage tag 'empty-room' (chair by a window, static shot). Fallback V1.

source.author: Blaise Pascal
source.verified_at: wording matched on two quotation sites; confirm in Gutenberg #18269 before posting

scripts.caption:
In a 2014 study (Wilson et al., Science), many people left alone with their thoughts for 15 minutes chose to give themselves a mild electric shock rather than sit there. Two thirds of the men did it at least once.

The urge to grab the phone isn't weakness. It's what quiet feels like when you're out of practice. Five minutes tonight, nothing in your hands.

How long did you last?

— Moodius
scripts.first_comment: Start with two minutes if five is too much. It's a muscle.

scripts.hook: Nobody tells you grief comes back in the supermarket.
scripts.hook_b: Grief doesn't end. It changes shape. One line helped me.
cards: Nobody tells you grief comes back in the supermarket.
Their cereal. Their song in a shop. Out of nowhere.
Epictetus offered one sentence for it:
“Never say about anything, ‘I have lost it,’ but rather ‘I have restored it.’”
It doesn't make it hurt less. It makes the time you had a gift, not a theft.
Send this to someone having a hard month.
scripts.visual: V2 footage tag 'aisle' (soft-focus shop aisle or fridge light) at 80% Slate overlay. Fallback V1. No sad-face imagery.
scripts.caption:
Grief isn't a stage you finish. It turns up in ordinary places, at ordinary times, and it doesn't ask.

Epictetus' line won't fix that, and it isn't meant to. It just changes the question from "why was this taken?" to "how lucky was I to have it at all?" Some days that helps. Some days it doesn't, and that's fine too.

If you're carrying one right now, you can just leave a 🤍 below.

— Moodius
scripts.first_comment: If it's been months and it's not moving at all, talking to someone (a GP, a counsellor, a grief line) isn't weakness. It's maintenance.

scripts.hook: You rehearse the lie in the shower first.
scripts.hook_b: The most dangerous lies are the ones you tell yourself.
cards: You rehearse the lie in the shower first.
“I'm just busy.” “I don't really care.” “I'll start when things calm down.”
Dostoevsky put the warning in an old monk's mouth:
The Brothers Karamazov, Book II ch. 2 · tr. Constance Garnett
Pick one sentence you say a lot. Is it true?
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate. Card 2 lines appear one at a time.

source.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source.section: Book II, ch. 2 'The Old Buffoon' (Father Zossima to Fyodor Pavlovitch)

scripts.caption:
The lies that cost the most aren't the ones you tell other people. They're the small, reasonable ones you tell yourself until they sound like facts.

Dostoevsky's elder goes on to say that the man who lies to himself ends up unable to see the truth in himself or anyone else. That's the real price.

Which sentence did you think of?

— Moodius
scripts.first_comment: You don't have to fix it tonight. Just stop saying it as if it's true.

scripts.hook: People I've said 'I'm fine' to:
scripts.hook_b: "I'm fine" might be the lie you tell most. Here's what it costs.
cards: A dentist with both hands in my mouth.
Putting a feeling into words, even silently, is linked to it calming down.
Send this to your most “fine” friend.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate. List cards 2-4 stack under the hook (previous lines stay at 60% opacity) for the comic rhythm.

source.author: Lieberman, Eisenberger, Crockett et al.
source.section: labelling an emotion reduced amygdala response to emotional images

scripts.caption:
"Fine" is a word that ends conversations, including the one you're supposed to have with yourself.

In a 2007 brain-imaging study, simply naming the emotion in a picture dampened the brain's alarm response. You don't need a speech. One accurate word is enough to get a bit of distance.

What's the honest word for today?

— Moodius
scripts.first_comment: Tired. Flat. Wound up. Proud, actually. Pick one.

scripts.hook: Me: I'll start Monday.
scripts.hook_b: The emperor of Rome hated getting up too. He wrote this.
cards: The emperor of Rome had the same mornings. He wrote himself this:
“In the morning when thou risest unwillingly, let this thought be present—I am rising to the work of a human being.”
Not a new you. Just today's work.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate.
scripts.caption:
Marcus goes on in the same passage to argue with himself about staying under the covers because it's warmer. The most powerful man alive, losing to his duvet.

The point isn't to become a morning person. It's to stop waiting for Monday to hand you a new identity. You get up for today's work, that's all.

What time did you actually get up today?

— Moodius
scripts.first_comment: Meditations 5.1 continues: "But this is more pleasant." He knew.

scripts.hook: 'Stoic' doesn't mean cold.
scripts.hook_b: You've been told Stoics don't feel. Marcus wrote the opposite.
cards: Marcus wrote down what he learned from his teacher Sextus:
“…entirely free from passion, and also most affectionate.”
Not ruled by your feelings. Still full of warmth. Both at once.
Send this to someone who thinks Stoic means silent.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate. 'Numb was never the goal.' with Ember rule.
scripts.caption:
The internet version of Stoicism is a man who feels nothing and texts in full stops. The original is someone who isn't pushed around by his moods and is still the warmest person in the room.

That's harder than being cold. Cold is easy.

Who's the most steady and kind person you know?

— Moodius
scripts.first_comment: In Stoic writing, "passion" means being carried away by a feeling, not having one.

scripts.hook: Got hurt once, so now nobody gets in?
scripts.hook_b: There are two ways to get trust wrong. Seneca named both.
cards: Got hurt once, so now nobody gets in?
Or you tell everyone everything on the first night?
“It is equally faulty to trust everyone and to trust no one.”
Trust is given in instalments. Let people earn the next one.
Save this before your next first date.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate.
scripts.caption:
Both of these feel like protection. One locks everyone out, the other skips the part where you find out who someone is.

Seneca's middle path: take your time deciding, then trust properly once you have. Small pieces, earned.

Which one are you more likely to do?

— Moodius
scripts.first_comment: Letters 3 also says: once you've decided someone is a friend, don't keep testing them.

scripts.hook: You improved so much you don't recognise yourself.
scripts.hook_b: Self-improvement can make you less yourself. Nietzsche saw it.
cards: You improved so much you don't recognise yourself.
New routine, new diet, new opinions. All borrowed from people you've never met.
“What saith thy conscience?—‘Thou shalt become what thou art.’”
The Gay Science 270 · tr. Thomas Common
Become yourself. Not a podcast host's version of you.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate.
scripts.caption:
There's a point in self-improvement where you stop growing and start copying. Somebody's morning, somebody's opinions, somebody's idea of a man.

Nietzsche's line isn't "become better". It's "become what you are": the thing that was already there before the noise.

What's one habit you picked up that never felt like you?

— Moodius
scripts.first_comment: Keep what works. Drop what you're only doing because someone with a microphone said so.

scripts.hook: Your job is the rock. Monday is the hill.
scripts.hook_b: Camus found the only way to be happy pushing a rock forever.
cards: Your job is the rock. Monday is the hill.
Camus took the bleakest myth there is, a man pushing a rock uphill forever,
and argued the man could still be happy.
Idea: Albert Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus (1942) · Moodius words
Not because the rock starts meaning something. Because he stops waiting for it to.
Send this to a fellow rock pusher.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate, or V2 tag 'stairs' (feet climbing a stairwell).

source.author: Albert Camus
source.translation: no quotation used (translations still in copyright)

scripts.caption:
Feeling behind usually comes with a hidden demand: that the effort should feel meaningful before you put it in.

Camus didn't promise the rock would stop rolling back. He said the man pushing it, fully awake to how absurd it is, can still own the push.

What's your rock this month?

— Moodius
scripts.first_comment: Camus wrote this in 1942, in the middle of a war. Not an easy time to call anything happy.

scripts.hook: Waiting to feel purpose before you start?
scripts.hook_b: A man who survived Auschwitz found three sources of meaning. None is a feeling.
cards: Waiting to feel purpose before you start?
Viktor Frankl, who survived the camps, saw meaning come from three places:
Something you do. Someone you love. How you carry what you can't change.
Idea: Viktor Frankl, Man's Search for Meaning (1946) · Moodius words
None of them start with a feeling. All of them start with you.
Save this. Pick one of the three today.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate. Card 4 shows the three items one per line, Ember dot before each.

source.author: Viktor Frankl
source.section: Part Two, 'The Meaning of Life' (creating a work or deed; experiencing something or someone; attitude to unavoidable suffering)

scripts.caption:
Purpose is rarely a feeling that arrives and then sends you into action. More often it's the other way round: you do something, love someone, or carry something heavy with some dignity, and the meaning shows up behind you.

Frankl saw this in the worst conditions a person can face.

Which of the three is strongest in your life right now?

— Moodius
scripts.first_comment: If none of them feel strong, start with the first. Something small, done properly, today.

scripts.hook: Their opinion of you is their homework.
scripts.hook_b: People pleasers do other people's homework. Here's how to stop.
cards: Their opinion of you is their homework.
The Courage to Be Disliked, built on Adler, asks one question when you're stuck: whose task is this?
Idea: Kishimi & Koga, The Courage to Be Disliked (2013) · Moodius words
Doing your part well: your task. Whether they like it: theirs.
Send this to a people pleaser.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate. Card 5 split into two lines, 'your task' and 'theirs' with a thin Ember rule between them.
scripts.caption:
A lot of anxiety is just doing someone else's work for them: managing their mood, predicting their reaction, editing yourself in advance.

Adler's test is plain. Who lives with the result of this choice? If it's them, it's their task. You can be kind. You can't do it for them.

Whose homework have you been doing lately?

— Moodius
scripts.first_comment: Epictetus would call this the line between what's up to you and what isn't. Same idea, 1,900 years apart.

scripts.hook: Your brain says 'you're a failure' like it's breaking news.
scripts.hook_b: Five words that make a cruel thought lose its grip.
cards: Your brain says “you're a failure” like it's breaking news.
It isn't news. It's a rerun.
Try putting five words in front of it:
“I'm having the thought that… I'm a failure.”
Idea: Russ Harris, The Happiness Trap (2007) · defusion, from ACT
Same thought. A little distance. Enough to choose what you do next.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate. Card 4: the five added words in Ash, 'I'm a failure.' in Bone.

source.author: Russ Harris
source.section: cognitive defusion ('I'm having the thought that…')

scripts.caption:
Thoughts arrive sounding like facts. "You're behind." "You'll mess this up." "Nobody cares."

You don't have to argue with them. Just notice them as thoughts. Adding "I'm having the thought that…" won't delete it, but it puts you back in the room as the one who decides.

What's your brain's most repeated headline?

— Moodius
scripts.first_comment: Funny version: say the thought in a cartoon voice. Harris suggests that one too. It works annoyingly well.

scripts.hook: You keep ruining good things right before they work.
scripts.hook_b: Self-sabotage isn't random. It's protecting something.
cards: You keep ruining good things right before they work.
The job you quit at month three. The person you pushed away when it got real.
Brianna Wiest's idea: self-sabotage is often a way of meeting a need you haven't admitted. Usually, staying safe in what's familiar.
Idea: Brianna Wiest, The Mountain Is You (2020) · Moodius words
Next time you feel the urge to wreck it, ask: what am I protecting?
Save this. You'll need it at month three.
scripts.visual: V1 flat Slate.

source.author: Brianna Wiest
source.section: self-sabotage as an unconscious way of meeting a need / staying in the familiar

scripts.caption:
When good things start working, part of you gets nervous, because good is unfamiliar and unfamiliar feels like danger. So you pull the plug and call it bad luck or bad timing.

The question that breaks the pattern isn't "what's wrong with me?" It's "what is this protecting me from?"

What's your month-three move?

— Moodius
scripts.first_comment: Usually the answer is: being seen trying, and failing anyway.

scripts.hook: Scrolling isn't rest. It's being entertained while exhausted.
scripts.hook_b: You rested for two hours and feel worse. Here's why.
cards: Two hours later you're more tired, and nothing in you got to stop.
Rest is the part where your mind goes quiet. A walk. A shower. Staring at a wall, honestly.
Ten minutes with nothing in your hands.
Save this. Try it before bed.
scripts.visual: V2 footage tag 'hallway-night' (hand placing phone face down; or a dark hallway). Fallback V1.
scripts.caption:
The scroll feels like a break because your body is still. But your attention is working the whole time, switching every few seconds, reacting to things it didn't choose.

Real rest is boring on purpose. Ten minutes of it does more than two hours of the other kind.

What's your version of staring at a wall?

— Moodius
scripts.first_comment: If you have ADHD, the wall might be a walk. Movement counts as quiet.
